name: Fender Champ (5F1)
notes: ~5W single-ended output stage with 1x6V6GT power tube and 5Y3 rectifier. The simplest classic Fender circuit, produced 1957–1964; an ideal first study schematic.

name: Fender Deluxe (5E3)
notes: ~15W cathode-biased push-pull amp with 2x6V6GT. Annotated by Rob Robinette; famous for interactive controls and early breakup. Produced 1955–1960.

name: Fender Bassman (5F6-A)
notes: ~45W fixed-bias push-pull amp with 4x6L6GC. The direct ancestor of the Marshall JTM45 and virtually every high-gain amp that followed. Produced 1958–1960.

name: Fender Bandmaster (5E7)
notes: ~30W push-pull amp with 3x6L6GC and a cathodyne phase inverter. Produced 1955–1960 in a tweed piggyback cabinet; an unusual three-power-tube design.

name: Fender Twin (5D8)
notes: ~80W tweed combo with 4x6L6GC — the loudest amp of its era. This is the full 1957 Twin service manual PDF including schematic and layout.

name: Fender Vibrolux (5F11)
notes: ~10W cathode-biased push-pull amp with 2x6V6GT and built-in tremolo. Produced 1956–1961; shares its core architecture with the 5E3 Deluxe.

name: Fender Princeton (6G2)
notes: ~12W brownface combo with 2x6V6GT, fixed bias, and tremolo. Produced 1961–1963; a transitional circuit bridging tweed and blackface tonal character.

name: Fender Deluxe (6G3)
notes: ~15W brownface Deluxe with 2x6V6GT and tube-driven tremolo. Produced 1961–1963; the 6G3 is distinctive for its smooth warm tone before the blackface era.

name: Fender Bassman (6G6-B)
notes: ~50W brownface Bassman with 4x6L6GC, fixed bias. Produced 1961–1963; a key transitional circuit between the famous tweed 5F6-A and the blackface models.

name: Fender Bandmaster (6G7-A)
notes: ~40W brownface piggyback with 2x6L6GC and tube tremolo. Produced 1961–1963; features a long-tail pair phase inverter distinct from the earlier tweed 5E7.

name: Fender Deluxe Reverb (AB763)
notes: ~22W push-pull amp with 2x6V6GT, spring reverb, and vibrato. The quintessential studio and recording combo; the AB763 circuit defines the blackface era.

name: Fender Princeton Reverb (AA1164)
notes: ~12W single-channel amp with 2x6V6GT, reverb, and vibrato. Produced 1964–1967; beloved for warm, compressed tone at practice and session volumes.

name: Fender Vibrolux Reverb (AB568)
notes: ~35W 2x10 combo with 2x6L6GC, reverb, and vibrato. Produced mid-1960s; the AB568 is a less common but highly regarded blackface circuit.

name: Fender Super Reverb (AA763)
notes: ~45W 4x10 combo with 2x6L6GC, reverb, and vibrato. Produced 1964–1966; a Chicago blues and R&B studio staple, known for glassy highs and punchy mids.

name: Fender Twin Reverb (AB763)
notes: ~85W 2x12 combo with 4x6L6GC; the loudest and cleanest blackface amp. Full '65 Twin Reverb service manual containing the complete AB763 schematic.

name: Marshall JTM45
notes: ~45W fixed-bias push-pull amp derived directly from the Fender 5F6-A Bassman, with 2xKT66 and GZ34 rectifier. Marshall's first production amp, circa 1962–1966.

name: Marshall 1962 Bluesbreaker
notes: ~45W 2x12 combo version of the JTM45 circuit, made famous by Eric Clapton on the John Mayall 'Beano' album in 1966. Uses 2xKT66 and GZ34 rectifier.

name: Marshall JTM100 Tremolo (1966)
notes: ~100W 1966 head with 4xEL34 and tremolo channel — an early high-power variant before the model stabilised as the 1959 Super Lead. Very rare in original form.

name: Marshall JMP Lead & Bass (1964)
notes: Early JMP-era schematic showing both the lead and bass channel on one drawing. A key reference for understanding the transition from JTM45 to the plexi designs.

name: Marshall 1959 Super Lead 100W (Plexi)
notes: ~100W head with 4xEL34; the definitive Plexi Super Lead that powered classic rock. This schematic covers the JCM800-era 1959 iteration of the same circuit.

name: Marshall 1987 50W Lead (Plexi)
notes: ~50W JMP-era Plexi head with 2xEL34. The 50W sibling of the 100W 1959, prized for its tighter feel and lower noise floor; produced through the early 1970s.

name: Marshall 1987 MkII JMP 50W
notes: ~50W MkII revision of the JMP 1987 with 2xEL34. Introduced detail-level circuit revisions over the original Plexi; produced through the late 1970s.

name: Marshall 1986 Bass 50W
notes: ~50W JMP Bass head with 2xEL34, voiced slightly darker than the lead model. Many guitarists favour it for its rounder character; shares core topology with the 1987.

name: Marshall 18 Watt
notes: ~18W combo or head with 2xEL84, produced 1965–1968. Shares circuit lineage with the Vox AC15 and is prized for touch-sensitive dynamics and early breakup.

name: Marshall JMP 50W Lead (1987)
notes: ~50W JMP Lead head schematic direct from Schematic Heaven's Marshall archive. A clean reference copy of the 1987 circuit useful alongside the El34World GIF version.

name: Vox AC4
notes: ~4W single-ended Class A combo with 1xEL84. Produced in the early 1960s; the simplest Vox circuit, sharing the characteristic EL84 chime of its larger siblings.

name: Vox AC10
notes: ~10W push-pull Class A combo with 2xEL84, produced 1958 to mid-1960s. Features an EF86 pentode input stage and the signature Vox Top Cut tone control.

name: Vox AC15 (1959)
notes: ~15W push-pull Class A combo with 2xEL84, one of the earliest production versions. Uses the original EF86 pentode front end, predating the 12AX7 Top Boost channel.

name: Vox AC15 (1960)
notes: ~15W push-pull Class A combo with 2xEL84. The 1960 version is an important transitional schematic showing the move toward the famous Top Boost voicing.

name: Vox AC30 (1960)
notes: ~30W push-pull Class A 2x12 combo with 4xEL84. The 1960 Top Boost circuit used by The Beatles and countless British Invasion bands; a landmark British amp design.

name: Vox AC50
notes: ~50W head with 2xEL34 in a fixed-bias push-pull configuration. Produced from 1963 onward; Vox's larger touring amp, used by major British acts of the 1960s.
